beats.script_body: More than a hundred years ago, Tchaikovsky himself presided over the opening performance of Carnegie Hall — just one of a legion of great musicians who have graced this famous stage. Across the decades the roster has run to stars like Anne-Sophie Mutter, Itzhak Perlman, Jon Batiste, and the Berliner Philharmoniker, all drawn by the unsurpassed acoustics and the honor of playing this magnificent hall.

physical_cues.cue: The famous stage of Carnegie Hall (daytime tours available Oct–June)

key_claims: Tchaikovsky presided over Carnegie Hall's opening performance more than 100 years ago
Performers have included Anne-Sophie Mutter, Itzhak Perlman, Jon Batiste, the Berliner Philharmoniker
beats.source_passage: Carnegie Hall More than 100 years ago, Tchaikovsky himself presided over the opening performance of Carnegie Hall, just one of a legion of great musicians who have graced this famous stage. Today, you may see such stars as Anne-Sophie Mutter, Itzhak Perlman, Daryl Hall and Todd Rundgren, Jon Batiste, the Berliner Philharmoniker, or more—all drawn by the unsurpassed acoustics and the honor of playing this magnificent hall (you can tour it Oct–June in the daytime; info on the web).

source_attribution.author: Pauline Frommer
source_attribution.chapter: Chapter 8: Theater, Classical Music & Landmark Venues

beats.script_body: There's a catch to dropping by this temple of music: the hall is often rented out by school groups, so it's no longer a guarantee that a great concert will be going on when you happen to be in town. And when there is a show, ticket prices ricochet up and down depending on the day of the week, the act, and the area in which you choose to sit.

beats.source_passage: Unfortunately, the hall is often rented out by school groups, so it’s no longer a guarantee that there will be a great concert going on when you’re in town. Ticket prices ricochet up and down, depending on the day of the week, the act, and, of course, the area in which you choose to sit.

source_attribution.chapter: Chapter 8: Theater, Classical Music & Landmark Venues

beats.script_body: Lincoln Center is a giant complex of theaters on the west side of Manhattan, flanking Columbus Avenue between 62nd and 65th streets. It hosts everything from major symphonic premieres to the Big Apple Circus, but it's most famous for its presentation of classic works of music, dance, opera, film, and theater. Toward that end it houses a number of permanent companies and plays host to the world's leading performing arts organizations.

beats.source_passage: Lincoln Center—a giant complex of theaters on the west side of Manhattan, flanking Columbus Avenue between 62nd and 65th streets—hosts everything from major symphonic premieres to the Big Apple Circus. It’s most famous for its presentation of classic works of music, dance, opera, film, and theater, and toward that end houses a number of permanent companies, as well as playing host to the world’s leading performing arts organizations.

source_attribution.author: Pauline Frommer
source_attribution.chapter: Chapter 8: Theater, Classical Music & Landmark Venues

beats.script_body: Behind these walls live some of the most storied names in American performing arts. The resident companies include the Chamber Music Society of Lincoln Center, the Film Society of Lincoln Center, and Lincoln Center Theater — the last of which houses both a well-respected Broadway theater and an off-Broadway theater. Among the center's other residents are the Metropolitan Opera, the New York City Ballet, the Juilliard School, the New York Philharmonic, and the American Ballet Theatre.

beats.source_passage: Resident companies include the Chamber Music Society of Lincoln Center (chambermusicsociety.org; 212/875-5788), the Film Society of Lincoln Center (filmlinc.com; 212/875-5601), and Lincoln Center Theater (lct.org; 212/362-7600), the latter of which houses both a well-respected Broadway theater and an off-Broadway theater. For details on the center’s other residents—the Metropolitan Opera, the New York City Ballet, the Juilliard School, the phenomenal New York Philharmonic, and the American Ballet Theatre—see “Classical Music, Opera & Dance” in this chapter.

beats.script_body: Everything about attending an opera here is grand — from the entrance you'll make, past monumental Chagall murals, to the world-class singers you'll hear, such as Joyce DiDonato or Roberto Alagna, to the pomp and glitz of the productions themselves. Sit La Bohème out in one of the Met's classic productions and you can't miss.

beats.source_passage: Metropolitan Opera             Everything about attending an opera here is grand—from the entrance you’ll make, past monumental Chagall murals, to the world-class singers you’ll hear (such as Joyce DiDonato or Roberto Alagna) to the pomp and glitz of the productions themselves. Though recent productions have received mixed reviews (one mentioned clunky scenery that, when moving, is louder than the singers), you can’t miss if you see La Bohème or another of the Met’s classic productions.

beats.script_body: Here's the lovely little secret about this house: the cheap seats get the best sound. Sit in the pricey orchestra section and you may have trouble making out the words, but buy a “family circle” seat way up high and the voices will float up to you in all their crystalline clarity. One warning, though — don't show up late. The Met does not seat latecomers; arrive after the curtain and you'll watch the first act on a video screen in the basement.

beats.script_body: In 2023 the music world was turned on its ear by the announcement that the New York Philharmonic had stolen wunderkind conductor Gustavo Dudamel from the Los Angeles Philharmonic. It was the classical music equivalent of when Tom Brady abandoned Boston for Tampa. Dudamel's tenure begins with the 2025/2026 season; most Phil concerts are performed in the acoustically excellent David Geffen Hall.

beats.script_body: The blockbuster modern dance shows tend to play the Joyce, and it's not hard to see why — it's simply the best space in the city to see dance, with not a bad seat in the house. In this renovated, Art Deco-era movie theater, the audience sits slightly above the dancers, so you won't be seeing just the feet or just the bodies; you'll get the whole picture. Pilobolus has played here, as well as the Limon Dance Company, Trisha Brown, and Savion Glover.

beats.script_body: The New York City Ballet was founded by Lincoln Kirstein and the twentieth century's greatest ballet choreographer, George Balanchine. It is for Balanchine's work that you still attend performances here at the David H. Koch Theater; his choreography is the staple, and it remains as diamond-sharp, elegant, and moving as when it was first performed as many as fifty years ago. Balanchine's version of The Nutcracker is a holiday classic and one of the most difficult tickets to get each Christmas season.

beats.script_body: American Ballet Theatre, which performs here at the Metropolitan Opera House, leans more on story ballets than the New York City Ballet does — Coppélia, Swan Lake, Sleeping Beauty — and tends to produce more bravura stars than NYCB, where the emphasis is on ensemble work. Its biggest draw is Misty Copeland, the United States' first Black prima ballerina.

beats.script_body: It's a thrill just to walk into the legendary but intimate Apollo Theater, past the collage of all the greats who've played here. Built in 1914, it looks much bigger on TV. Perhaps most famous for launching the careers of Ella Fitzgerald, Aretha Franklin, and Duke Ellington, today it's mostly used for comedy shows and its weekly Amateur Night — a gladiatorial music battle where the winners may emerge stars and the losers are skewered with the unkindest of boos and shouted insults.

beats.script_body: They really knew how to build theaters back in the 1920s. Every seat at this Art Deco landmark has a good view, and the acoustics are remarkable — which may be why the Beacon is such a favorite of the touring bands who make it their New York home. You won't get the mega-names, but you will see talented stars either on the way up or down, names such as the Tedeschi Trucks Band, Jackson Browne, Ringo Starr, and comedians Jerry Seinfeld and Eddie Izzard.

beats.script_body: Outside of Manhattan, BAM is the finest of the multiuse facilities — along with the Park Avenue Armory, it may well be the best place in the United States for challenging, inventive, and acclaimed international productions of music, dance, performance art, and theater. It's at BAM where you'll see highbrow theater straight from the West End, like James McAvoy in Cyrano de Bergerac, Hannah Gadsby's new comedy show, or a Phillip Glass symphony.

beats.script_body: This small theater, just 125 seats, is set on an actual barge moored near the Brooklyn Bridge, with big views of the Manhattan skyline and acoustics to die for. Pianissimos are more piano here and fortissimos molto-loud, even when played by a solo piano or string quartet. It's one of the few truly intimate stages in the city, and the prices are intimate too, starting at just $35.

beats.script_body: This colossal former military space, with a 55,000-square-foot drill hall at its core, has made a name for itself in recent years for the prestige, scope — often huge — and quirkiness of the shows it has produced and brought in from all corners of the globe. They've included Robert Icke's Olivier Award-winning production The Doctor with Juliet Stevenson, several large pieces by the doyenne of French theater Ariane Mnouchkine, and new dance works by Anne Teresa de Keersmaeker.

beats.source_passage: Park Avenue Armory              This colossal former military space, with a 55,000-square-foot drill hall at its core, has made a name for itself in recent years for the prestige, scope (often huuuge), and quirkiness of the shows it has produced and/or brought in from all corners of the globe. They’ve included director Robert Icke’s Olivier Award–winning production The Doctor (with Juliet Stevenson), several large pieces by the doyenne of French theater Ariane Mnouchkine, new dance works by Anne Teresa de Keersmaeker, and dozens of musical recitals.

beats.script_body: It's hard to classify just what Joe's Pub is, beyond a very handsome space in a landmark building that hosts performances and serves strong cocktails and pub food. Its show roster is all over the map — spoken-word artists, rising singer/songwriters, jazz bands, pop stars, you name it. Past performers include Alicia Keys, fashion designer Isaac Mizrahi, Patti LuPone, and Wynton Marsalis.
